sources.text:
Bryan Kohberger has filed a petition seeking to withdraw his guilty plea in the Idaho murders case, arguing that he was misled into pleading guilty despite maintaining his innocence. Kohberger was convicted of killing four University of Idaho students in 2022. He is currently serving four life sentences after he pleaded guilty in July 2025.
Bryan Kohberger seeks to withdraw guilty plea after Idaho murders conviction
In a phone interview with The New York Times, the man convicted of killing four students claimed: “he is innocent and was misled into confessing to the high-profile killings”.
As per the report, Kohberger said, “My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, must be withdrawn.” However, the 31-year-old declined to comment on any specifics. He refused to discuss the evidence against him or why he agreed to enter a guilty plea if he is innocent.
In his handwritten post-conviction relief petition filed in Ada County, Kohberger wrote that “justice was not served” and “unanswered questions seem to multiply with each piece of discovery unsealed.”
Kohberger continued, “Circumnavigated by a broken plea, the trial never provided the public the clarity conducive to closure, and justice shall remain abjectly miscarried unless that plea is withdrawn.”
He further cited “ineffective assistance of counsel during criminal proceedings,” alleging his defense team failed to disclose or review evidence that could have helped his case.
The guilty plea marks a stunning shift from July 2025. At the time, Judge Steven Hippler directly asked Kohberger, “Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?” Kohberger answered, “Yes.” He did not provide a motive for the killings during the plea hearing.
Kohberger pleaded guilty in July 2025 to four counts of first-degree murder and 10 years for felony burglary. The plea deal spared him the death penalty in exchange for four consecutive life sentences without parole. He was also fined $270,000. Kohberger is serving his sentence at a maximum-security prison in Kuna, Idaho.

'It's Just Funny': Idaho 4 Victim's Mom Slams Bryan Kohberger's Plan to Change Plea as 'Just Judicial Games'
July 28 2026, Published 12:34 p.m. ET
Bryan Kohberger's choice to change his plea was a red flag to the mother of an Idaho 4 victim.
While the 31-year-old originally pled guilty to killing four students in Moscow, Idaho, he's now petitioned the court to withdraw that plea in a highly unusual legal move. However, Kristi Goncalves, 48, the mother of victim Kaylee Goncalves, sees no "merit" in Kohberger's recent choice, RadarOnline.com has learned.
Kristi Goncalves Speaks Out Against Bryan Kohberger's Request
Goncalves, 48, instead, claimed Kohberger was "just judicial games."
She told Newsweek, “America has seen our family go through pain for many, many years now. It wasn’t the news we wanted to wake up to today."
Kohberger pleaded guilty publicly in court, and the judge even confirmed it was because he believed himself to be guilty. However, he now alleged he was coerced into his plea. Goncalves, though, doesn't buy it.
"We're very confident that this will go nowhere," she said. "We're going to remain focused and we're going to remain positive."
Kohberger Claims He Was Lied To
Kohberger alleged his original plea was "induced by unkept promises" from his attorneys, who allegedly threatened him. In the court documents filed on Monday, Kohberger claimed the attorneys withheld evidence, which could show his innocence.
Further, he alleged his attorneys advised him his plea wasn't required to be true. In private, he claimed, he was in "vehement denial of actual guilt," but his attorneys allegedly informed him a guilty plea was for the better anyway.
They allegedly claimed he would receive better treatment. In Idaho, the death penalty is still on the table, but by pleading guilty, he managed to dodge an execution and opt for a life sentence.
However, his attorneys allegedly claimed a guilty plea would come with additional perks and privileges like immediate freedom of movement and employment. Plus, they allegedly promised he'd have immediate contact visits.
All of this, though, Kohberger called "elaborate lies."
Kohberger said in a statement to The New York Times, “My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn."
Nonetheless, Goncalves still doesn't see merit in Kohberger's attempt to change his plea. She said, "So for him to now say, you know, he didn't really know what he was getting himself into with the plea deal, it's just funny."
Idaho Attorney General Promises Pursuit of Justice
Idaho Attorney General Raúl R. Labrador vowed to continue fighting for justice in the case.
"My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana, and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news," he wrote on X. "My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out."
The families, too, are preparing for a renewed fight against Kohberger.
Gonclaves said, "But in the case that a judge were to accept it and give him a new trial, we're all for it. So either way, we're like, it is what it is."
Investigation Cluttered With Controversy
Kohberger previously pled guilty to four counts of first-degree murder and one count of felony burglary after allegedly killing Ethan Chapin, 20; Kaylee Goncalves, 21; Xana Kernodle, 20; and Madison Mogen, 21, in a case dubbed the "Idaho 4."
They were killed in an off-campus home at the University of Idaho. The group was roommates, with only two housemates, Bethany Funke and Dylan Mortensen, surviving the attack. She locked herself in her room after checking on a noise in the apartment and seeing a masked figure.
Mortensen did not make a phone call to 911 during the attack because she was allegedly intoxicated. When she left her room, she ran into Kernodle unconscious, but Mortensen believed her to just be intoxicated, too. After seeing Funke, the pair locked themselves in a room and called for help in the morning. It was too late, as all victims were pronounced dead on the scene.
The murderer's motive remains a mystery.
The investigation was shrouded in controversy, especially after police ignored policy and used ancestral genealogical websites GEDmatch and MyHeritage for DNA found at the scene. Typically, investigators are limited to using only databases "that provide explicit notice to their service users and the public that law enforcement may use their service sites."
Kohberger was arrested after he was observed wearing surgical gloves and putting trash bags in a neighbor's garbage can. When authorities searched his home, they discovered a knife, a pistol, and a black face mask.

'A narcissist' - victim's family blasts Kohberger for challenging Idaho murder conviction
The family of one of the victims of Bryan Kohberger has hit out after it emerged that he was challenging his conviction for four murders of students in the US state of Idaho.
Kohberger was sentenced last year to four consecutive terms of life in prison after pleading guilty to charges of murder in the November 2022 killings.
In recent days, Kohberger told the New York Times he was taking back his plea, which was made to avoid the death penalty. He said it had rested on "false promises and blatant disinformation".
The family of Kaylee Goncalves, one of the students who was killed, said that Kohberger was a "narcissist", who appeared to have changed his position.
"He chose not to leave his fate - or the facts of the case - to a jury," the statement from the Goncalves family said.
"He never cried foul, never claimed he was uninformed or pressured, and never suggested there were problems with the discovery materials he and his counsel had reviewed for two years that should have been challenged."
The Goncalves family went on to say "the real tragedy" was the amount of attention that Kohberger was now receiving at the expense of the victims.
Kohberger was convicted of stabbing to death housemates Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen, who all attended the University of Idaho, in their off-campus home on 13 November 2022.
The case shocked the small student town of Moscow and made national headlines for almost two months before Kohberger was arrested.
Kohberger was a criminology doctorate student at a different institution, Washington State University.
He never shared a motive with the court and it is not clear why he drove to another campus to brutally stab four students.
Investigators were unable to link him to the victims, although they presented compelling evidence that put him at the scene of the crime.
In his statement to the New York Times, declaring his new intention to enter a not-guilty plea, Kohberger protested his innocence and said he was offering prosecutors another chance to file for the death penalty if they wanted to.
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador paid tribute to the victims' families, saying they had "already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today's deeply painful news".
Labrador's statement added: "My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out."
But Kohberger's attempt to reverse his plea is a longshot, experts say.
"He told the judge under oath at the plea hearing that he understood the deal, was acting voluntarily, and was pleading guilty because he was guilty," Sam Newton, associate professor at University of Idaho College of Law, told the BBC.
"That's a real problem, since courts don't take kindly to walking a voluntary plea back without hard proof that something went seriously wrong behind the scenes."

sources.news_title: Man convicted in Idaho college killings seeks to take back guilty plea
sources.text:
Man convicted in Idaho college killings seeks to take back guilty plea
The criminology student convicted last year of murdering four University of Idaho students in their home is seeking to abandon his guilty plea and obtain a trial, claiming he is innocent and was misled into confessing to the high-profile killings.
In an interview with The New York Times, Bryan Kohberger, who is currently serving four life sentences, said he had filed a petition challenging his conviction, citing concerns about how the plea deal came together.
“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” Kohberger said in a statement provided to the Times on Sunday night. He reiterated in a phone call from prison in Idaho that he had an “absolute claim of innocence.”
Kohberger had not granted an interview or made public comments before speaking with the Times. He declined to discuss any evidence or other specific details related to his innocence claim, as well as the specific concerns he had about the plea process. It is rare for defendants to win post-conviction challenges.
The family of Kaylee Goncalves, one of the victims, said in a statement that Kohberger was like a “mosquito you just can’t seem to swat.”
“The real tragedy is this: If even a fraction of the energy spent trying to free a guilty man were directed toward honoring the victims, there would be statues of them on every corner, parks bearing their names, and days set aside to remember the lives they lost at the hands of a narcissist,” the statement read.
The Latah County Prosecutor’s Office did not return a call seeking comment. Idaho Attorney General Raul Labrador released a statement saying his heart went out to the victims’ families, noting they had “already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news.”
“My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out,” he said.
In November 2022, the four murders in Moscow, Idaho, a college town that had not seen a homicide in seven years, captivated the country for weeks as investigators struggled to identify a suspect. Kohberger’s arrest brought relief to the community but also stoked further mystery and speculation, as investigators never identified a motive or any previous relationship with the victims.
In court, law enforcement officials outlined the evidence against Kohberger. His DNA was found on a Ka-Bar knife sheath that had been left next to two of the victims. Amazon records showed he had purchased a Ka-Bar knife and sheath months prior. He drove a white Elantra, the type of car that investigators determined had been on surveillance video circling the crime scene and then speeding away from it. Kohberger’s phone showed he was out that night, with his phone turned off at the time of the murders.
Kohberger declined to discuss the evidence against him in his call with the Times. He said, “The intention is for all of those questions to be investigated and answered appropriately in a trial setting.”
Kohberger, who had court-appointed representation throughout the case, ending with his guilty plea, said he prepared the documentation to challenge the case on his own. He requested to have a lawyer appointed to help him going forward.
After he was arrested in December 2022, Kohberger’s initial lawyer said his client was eager to be exonerated. Court-appointed lawyers spent more than two years challenging the evidence collected against Kohberger, only for a surprise plea deal to come together a few weeks before a trial was to begin.
Kohberger accepted responsibility for the murders at a July 2025 hearing. He was not required to offer a motive for the killings — and never has. The lack of a detailed confession outraged some of the victims’ family members and even President Donald Trump, who had called on the judge to demand an explanation from Kohberger.
In court, the judge asked Kohberger, “Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?”
“Yes,” Kohberger responded. He later sat in silence at a sentencing hearing at which family members of the victims expressed their grief and anger.
In the early morning hours of Nov. 13, 2022, after a typical Saturday night out, the four victims were stabbed to death in an off-campus home. The bodies of Madison Mogen, 21, and Goncalves, 21, were found together in a bed on the home’s third floor. The bodies of Xana Kernodle, 20, and her boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, 20, were found in a bedroom on the second floor.
One of the experts who worked on Kohberger’s defense team has taken particular issue with the plea arrangement and the evidence. Brent Turvey, a forensic scientist who analyzed the crime scene for the defense, argued that the crime was committed by multiple perpetrators, criticized how investigators documented evidence and questioned why more testing was not done of a hair found with one of the victims.
The lawyers who served as Kohberger’s defense team have rebuked Turvey, telling The Idaho Statesman that he “is now speaking about topics that are still confidential, many of which are outside of his areas of expertise.” The lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday. Turvey’s concerns were included in a book about the case, “Broken Plea.”
Kohberger alluded to those issues in his statement, saying that “unanswered questions seem to multiply with each piece of discovery unsealed.” He said he was OK that a new trial would mean the prospect of a potential death penalty.
“Why am I breaking my silence?” Kohberger said Sunday in the interview from the Idaho Maximum Security Institution, just south of Boise. “A lot went wrong in those plea discussions. I really do want that to be heard.”
In the plea agreement that Kohberger signed, he acknowledged that he “knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently waives all rights to appeal any and all issues in this case.” Still, defendants can make other claims about the legal process through post-conviction relief.

sources.news_title: Bryan Kohberger asks to withdraw guilty plea in University of Idaho murders case
sources.text:
BOISE, Idaho — The man convicted of murdering four University of Idaho students is asking a court to let him withdraw his guilty plea and go to trial, saying his attorneys manipulated him into making the deal by promising him better prison conditions and scaring him about the quality of life on death row.
Bryan Kohberger, 31, filed the hand-written petition on Monday from the Idaho Maximum Security Penitentiary where he is serving four consecutive life sentences for the murders of Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen in a rental home near campus in 2022. It's been just over one year since he pleaded guilty to the stabbing deaths that scarred the close-knit community of Moscow, Idaho.
In his request, Kohberger said his attorneys didn't adequately represent him and that his guilty plea wasn't knowingly or voluntarily entered because it "was induced by unkept promises" and threats.
He offered only a few details in elaboration, saying they failed to disclose or review evidence that might have helped his case during plea discussions, like an "unknown hair in Chapin's hand."
He also wrote that the attorneys insisted that his plea "need not be truthful, despite petitioner's vehement denial of actual guilt," that they promised life in prison would come with "immediate contact visits, freedom of movement, employment" and that they told him "elaborate lies of DR (death row) life."
That's the opposite of what Kohberger told 4th District Judge Steven Hippler on July 2, 2025, when he confirmed that he was pleading guilty "freely and voluntarily" because he was, in fact, guilty, and not because he had some other incentive. As part of that process, he had to agree to waive his rights to appeal, confirm that he understood the punishments on the table for the crimes and assure the court that he wasn't coerced by his attorneys or anyone else to make the plea.
Those and other questions were posed to Kohberger more than once — first in a nine-page legal document that Kohberger filled out, initialed and signed, and later in direct questioning by the judge — all in an effort to ensure that his plea would hold up.
In exchange for his plea, prosecutors agreed they would not seek the death penalty, and instead would recommend that he be sentenced to four back-to-back life sentences without the possibility of parole, plus an additional 10 years.
"Have any other promises been made to you that have influenced your decision to plead guilty?" Kohberger was asked on the plea agreement document. He checked the the box indicating "no."
"Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?" Hippler asked him in court a few days later.
"Yes," Kohberger replied.
Once a defendant has been sentenced, Idaho law requires them to show that they experienced "manifest injustice" in order to withdraw a guilty plea. That is a tough legal standard, but it can be met if a defendant convinces a judge that they made the plea involuntarily or that other serious constitutional errors were made in the case.
For Kohberger's team of four court-appointed attorneys, the plea deal was a way to save his life. Over two years of hearings, they tried multiple times to get capital punishment off the table. They challenged the legitimacy of DNA evidence, argued that Kohberger's autism diagnosis made him less culpable, suggested there might be another unknown suspect to be found, and said the death penalty violates international standards of decency.
But none of the arguments worked, and Kohberger's trial was just a month away when he reached the plea agreement.
The lead defense attorney on the case, Anne Taylor, is one of the most highly regarded capital defenders in the state, with nearly three decades of experience, more than half of it as a death-penalty-qualified defender. Is Bryan Kohberger Innocent? Murderer Claims He Was 'Convinced to Falsely Confess' to Idaho Student Killings
Idaho killer files bid to overturn guilty plea over alleged false confession
Bryan Kohberger, who pleaded guilty to the murders of four University of Idaho students as part of a plea agreement, is seeking to withdraw his guilty plea, claiming he was convinced to falsely confess.
The post-conviction filing has renewed public interest in whether Kohberger's conviction could face fresh legal scrutiny despite his previous admission of guilt in court.
The latest development could reopen one of America's most closely watched murder cases as a judge considers whether his plea was entered voluntarily and in accordance with the law.
Bryan Kohberger Seeks To Withdraw Guilty Plea
Court documents filed in Idaho on Monday show Kohberger has submitted a petition for post-conviction relief, asking the court to reopen his case and allow him to withdraw his guilty plea.
In the handwritten filing, Kohberger alleges he accepted the plea agreement because of 'threats', 'false promises' and inaccurate information provided during the legal process.
He also claims his defence team failed to disclose or review exculpatory evidence, arguing that he received ineffective assistance of counsel.
Kohberger further alleges he was given a 'gross misrepresentation' of what a life sentence without parole and death row in Idaho would involve before agreeing to plead guilty.
In a statement provided to The New York Times, he said: 'My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn.'
Although Kohberger waived his right to appeal as part of the plea agreement, legal experts note that defendants may still pursue post-conviction relief by challenging the validity of a guilty plea.
Why Bryan Kohberger Now Claims Innocence
The latest filing marks a sharp reversal from Kohberger's position during last year's plea hearing.
After initially pleading not guilty, the former Washington State University criminology PhD student accepted a plea deal that spared him the death penalty.
During the hearing, Judge Steven Hippler asked him: 'Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?'
Kohberger replied: 'Yes.'
He was subsequently sentenced to four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole for the murders of Ethan Chapin, 20, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Madison Mogen, 21, who were fatally stabbed at an off-campus home in Moscow, Idaho, on 13 November 2022.
Kohberger now argues that his admission of guilt was not voluntary and resulted from misleading advice and misinformation surrounding the plea agreement.
Evidence Presented in the Idaho Student Killings Case
The prosecution previously outlined a substantial body of evidence linking Kohberger to the Idaho student killings.
Investigators said DNA recovered from a knife sheath found on a bed near Madison Mogen matched Kohberger through investigative genetic genealogy.
Authorities later arrested him in Pennsylvania, more than a month after the killings, after forensic DNA testing of rubbish collected outside his family home helped establish probable cause.
Before the guilty plea, Kohberger's defence team maintained he had been driving alone on the night of the murders.
Because the case ended with a plea agreement, prosecutors were not required to present their evidence before a jury during a full criminal trial.
Victims' Families and Officials Respond
The latest court filing drew a swift response from the family of victim Kaylee Goncalves, who criticised Kohberger's attempt to withdraw his plea.
In a statement shared on Facebook, the family described him as 'the mosquito you just can't seem to swat'.
They noted Kohberger had previously admitted guilt in court and had not claimed at the time that he was pressured, misled or denied access to evidence.
The family also said they would welcome a trial, expressing confidence that Kohberger would face the death penalty if his guilty plea were successfully withdrawn.
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador also issued a statement expressing sympathy for the victims' families and said his office was prepared 'to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out'.
Meanwhile, the Latah County Prosecutor's Office declined to comment because the litigation remains pending, while one of Kohberger's former defence attorneys also declined to comment on the ongoing proceedings.

Man convicted of Idaho student killings seeks to retract guilty plea
The criminology student convicted last year of murdering four University of Idaho students in their home is seeking to abandon his guilty plea and obtain a trial, claiming he is innocent and was misled into confessing to the high-profile killings.
In an interview with The New York Times, Bryan Kohberger, who is serving four life sentences, said he had filed a petition challenging his conviction, citing concerns about how the plea deal came together.
“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” Kohberger said in a statement provided to the Times on Sunday night. He reiterated in a phone call from prison in Idaho that he had an “absolute claim of innocence”.
Kohberger had not granted an interview or made public comments before speaking with the Times. He declined to discuss any evidence or other specific details related to his claim of innocence, as well as the specific concerns he had about the plea process. It is rare for defendants to win post-conviction challenges.
The family of Kaylee Goncalves, one of the victims, said in a statement that Kohberger was like a “mosquito you just can’t seem to swat”.
“The real tragedy is this: If even a fraction of the energy spent trying to free a guilty man were directed toward honouring the victims, there would be statues of them on every corner, parks bearing their names, and days set aside to remember the lives they lost at the hands of a narcissist,” the statement read.
The Latah County Prosecutor’s Office did not return a call seeking comment. Idaho Attorney-General Raul Labrador released a statement saying his heart went out to the victims’ families, noting they had “already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news.”
“My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out,” he said.
In November 2022, the four murders in Moscow, Idaho, a college town that had not seen a homicide in seven years, captivated the country for weeks as investigators struggled to identify a suspect. Kohberger’s arrest brought relief to the community but also stoked further mystery and speculation, as investigators never identified a motive or any previous relationship with the victims.
In court, law enforcement officials outlined the evidence against Kohberger. His DNA was found on a Ka-Bar knife sheath that had been left next to two of the victims. Amazon records showed he had purchased a Ka-Bar knife and sheath months prior. He drove a white Hyundai Elantra, the type of car that investigators determined had been captured on surveillance video circling the crime scene before speeding away. Kohberger’s phone showed he was out that night, with his phone turned off at the time of the murders.
Kohberger declined to discuss the evidence against him in his call with the Times. He said: “The intention is for all of those questions to be investigated and answered appropriately in a trial setting.”
Kohberger, who had court-appointed representation throughout the case, ending with his guilty plea, said he prepared the documentation to challenge the case on his own. He requested that a lawyer be appointed to help him going forward.
After he was arrested in December 2022, Kohberger’s initial lawyer said his client was eager to be exonerated. Court-appointed lawyers spent more than two years challenging the evidence collected against Kohberger, only for a surprise plea deal to come together a few weeks before a trial was to begin.
Still no motive
Kohberger accepted responsibility for the murders at a July 2025 hearing. He was not required to offer a motive for the killings – and never has. The lack of a detailed confession outraged some of the victims’ family members and even US President Donald Trump, who had called on the judge to demand an explanation from Kohberger.
In court, the judge asked Kohberger: “Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?”
“Yes,” Kohberger responded. He later sat in silence at a sentencing hearing at which family members of the victims expressed their grief and anger.
In the early morning hours of November 13, 2022, after a typical Saturday night out, the four victims were stabbed to death in an off-campus home. The bodies of Madison Mogen, 21, and Goncalves, 21, were found together in a bed on the home’s third floor. The bodies of Xana Kernodle, 20, and her boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, 20, were found in a bedroom on the second floor.
One of the experts who worked on Kohberger’s defence team has taken particular issue with the plea arrangement and the evidence. Brent Turvey, a forensic scientist who analysed the crime scene for the defence, argued that the crime was committed by multiple perpetrators, criticised how investigators documented evidence and questioned why more testing was not done on a hair found with one of the victims.
‘A lot went wrong in those plea discussions. I really do want that to be heard.’Brian Kohberger
The lawyers who served as Kohberger’s defence team have rebuked Turvey, telling The Idaho Statesman that he “is now speaking about topics that are still confidential, many of which are outside of his areas of expertise”. The lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Turvey’s concerns were included in a book about the case, Broken Plea.
Kohberger alluded to those issues in his statement, saying that “unanswered questions seem to multiply with each piece of discovery unsealed”. He said he was OK that a new trial would mean the prospect of a potential death penalty.
“Why am I breaking my silence?” Kohberger said Sunday in the interview from the Idaho Maximum Security Institution, just south of Boise. “A lot went wrong in those plea discussions. I really do want that to be heard.”
In the plea agreement that Kohberger signed, he acknowledged that he “knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently waives all rights to appeal any and all issues in this case”. Still, defendants can make other claims about the legal process through post-conviction relief.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Bryan Kohberger seeks to withdraw guilty plea in Idaho murders
Bryan Kohberger, the man convicted of the murders of four Idaho college students in 2022, has filed a petition seeking to challenge his guilty plea and conviction, court records show.
Kohberger, 31, filed a "petition for post-conviction relief" July 27 in the Ada County District Court in Idaho. Such petitions allow defendants to challenge convictions after sentencing on grounds including ineffective assistance of counsel and other claimed legal or constitutional errors. Court records indicate Kohberger is representing himself.
Kohberger first publicly disclosed the petition in an interview with The New York Times, in which he claimed he was innocent and had been misled into confessing to the high-profile killings. He declined to discuss evidence supporting his claim of innocence or elaborate on his concerns about the plea process, according to The Times.
"Circumnavigated by a broken plea, the trial never provided the public the clarity conducive to closure, and justice shall remain abjectly miscarried unless that plea is withdrawn. ... My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn," he said in a statement to the newspaper July 26.
Last year, Kohberger pleaded guilty to the murders of University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20, at an off-campus home in Moscow, Idaho, in November 2022. He was sentenced to four life sentences without the possibility of parole and a 10-year sentence for burglary.
What happened in the 2022 Idaho killings?
Prosecutors said Kohberger broke into the victims' rental home near the University of Idaho campus and stabbed the four students to death on Nov. 13, 2022. The murders rocked the town of Moscow, setting the community on edge as investigators searched for weeks for a suspect before authorities arrested Kohberger on Dec. 30, 2022, in Pennsylvania, where his family lives.
Kohberger was linked to the crimes using DNA evidence found on a knife sheath near one of the victims' bodies, along with cell phone data and surveillance footage of his car's movements, according to prosecutors.
At the time of the killings, Kohberger was a doctoral student in criminal justice at nearby Washington State University. Police records reviewed by USA TODAY last year detailed a history of complaints about Kohberger's behavior at the university, including allegations he intimidated classmates and made female students feel "unsafe."
Kohberger struck a plea deal in July 2025 that divided the victims' families because it allowed him to avoid the death penalty and a highly publicized trial. The plea agreement was announced just weeks before his murder trial was set to begin in August 2025.
Though Kohberger admitted responsibility for the killings during his plea hearing, he never publicly explained a motive. In his statement to The Times, he called investigators’ account of the killings a "myopic narrative" and a "work of fiction," arguing that its “faulty premises were never challenged at trial."
Idaho victim's family criticizes Kohberger's innocence claims
In response to Kohberger's filing, Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said his office "stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out."
"My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana, and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news," Labrador said in a statement on X.
The Goncalves family also criticized The Times for giving Kohberger a platform to share his claims of innocence. In a statement July 27, the family described Kohberger as a "mosquito you just can’t seem to swat."
"The story didn’t have much else in it, other than a guilty man claiming he is innocent once again," the Goncalves family said in the statement. "Nothing in the story or in Kohberger's statement does he allude to the fact [that] he did not 'knowingly, voluntarily and intelligently' admit to murdering the 4 victims of this tragedy."
The family said Kohberger chose not to leave his fate to a jury and avoided a potential death sentence by pleading guilty. They added they were prepared for any additional court proceedings and remained confident in the evidence against Kohberger.
"The Defendant will get another day in court," the Goncalves family said. "A nice break from his solitary confinement, getting to go for a ride, maybe some different food, photos taken and the attention all back on him and his 'innocence'."

sources.news_title: 'Threats' and 'unkept promises' : Why convicted killer Bryan Kohberger says he deserves a trial in UI student murders
Bryan Kohberger asks to withdraw his guilty plea in the University of Idaho murders case
sources.text:
Bryan Kohberger asks to withdraw his guilty plea in the University of Idaho murders case
BOISE, Idaho (AP) — The man convicted of murdering four University of Idaho students is asking a court to let him withdraw his guilty plea and go to trial, saying his attorneys manipulated him into making the deal by promising him better prison conditions and scaring him about the quality of life on death row.
Bryan Kohberger, 31, filed the hand-written petition on Monday from the Idaho Maximum Security Penitentiary where he is serving four consecutive life sentences for the murders of Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen in a rental home near campus in 2022. It’s been just over one year since he pleaded guilty to the stabbing deaths that scarred the close-knit community of Moscow, Idaho.
In his request, Kohberger said his attorneys didn’t adequately represent him and that his guilty plea wasn’t knowingly or voluntarily entered because it “was induced by unkept promises” and threats.
He offered only a few details in elaboration, saying they failed to disclose or review evidence that might have helped his case during plea discussions, like an “unknown hair in Chapin’s hand.”
He also wrote that the attorneys insisted that his plea “need not be truthful, despite petitioner’s vehement denial of actual guilt,” that they promised life in prison would come with “immediate contact visits, freedom of movement, employment” and that they told him “elaborate lies of DR (death row) life.”
That’s the opposite of what Kohberger told 4th District Judge Steven Hippler on July 2, 2025, when he confirmed that he was pleading guilty “freely and voluntarily” because he was, in fact, guilty, and not because he had some other incentive. As part of that process, he had to agree to waive his rights to appeal, confirm that he understood the punishments on the table for the crimes and assure the court that he wasn’t coerced by his attorneys or anyone else to make the plea.
Those and other questions were posed to Kohberger more than once — first in a nine-page legal document that Kohberger filled out, initialed and signed, and later in direct questioning by the judge — all in an effort to ensure that his plea would hold up.
In exchange for his plea, prosecutors agreed they would not seek the death penalty, and instead would recommend that he be sentenced to four back-to-back life sentences without the possibility of parole, plus an additional 10 years.
“Have any other promises been made to you that have influenced your decision to plead guilty?” Kohberger was asked on the plea agreement document. He checked the the box indicating “no.”
“Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?” Hippler asked him in court a few days later.
“Yes,” Kohberger replied.
Once a defendant has been sentenced, Idaho law requires them to show that they experienced “manifest injustice” in order to withdraw a guilty plea. That is a tough legal standard, but it can be met if a defendant convinces a judge that they made the plea involuntarily or that other serious constitutional errors were made in the case.
For Kohberger’s team of four court-appointed attorneys, the plea deal was a way to save his life. Over two years of hearings, they tried multiple times to get capital punishment off the table. They challenged the legitimacy of DNA evidence, argued that Kohberger’s autism diagnosis made him less culpable, suggested there might be another unknown suspect to be found, and said the death penalty violates international standards of decency.
But none of the arguments worked, and Kohberger’s trial was just a month away when he reached the plea agreement.
The lead defense attorney on the case, Anne Taylor, is one of the most highly regarded capital defenders in the state, with nearly three decades of experience, more than half of it as a death-penalty-qualified defender. A person who answered the phone at her office on Monday immediately said “no comment” and hung up before she could be asked if it was Kohberger’s case or another matter on which she was declining to comment.

Kohberger remains housed at Idaho's only maximum-security prison, in the same unit as death row inmates including Chad Daybell, where he has separately raised complaints about food options and treatment by fellow inmates.
Kohberger's attempt to withdraw a guilty plea nearly a year after entering it, and just days after his formal sentencing, represents an unusually difficult legal path given Idaho's manifest-injustice standard, which generally requires far more than a defendant's later change of heart or renewed claims of innocence, particularly when that defendant explicitly affirmed guilt under oath during the plea colloquy itself. The move reopens a case that had appeared fully and finally resolved after Kohberger's guilty plea and sentencing, forcing the victims' families to revisit legal proceedings many had treated as concluded, a burden reflected sharply in the Goncalves family's public response. Prosecutors' apparent openness, framed through Kohberger's own account, to potentially seeking the death penalty again if the case reopens raises the stakes of the filing considerably beyond a routine post-conviction motion, since a successful withdrawal could ultimately expose Kohberger to a capital trial he avoided through his original plea deal.
An Idaho court will need to rule on whether Kohberger's petition meets the legal threshold to reopen the case and withdraw his plea, a process that could take weeks or months given the complexity of the ineffective-assistance claim he is expected to raise. Prosecutors are expected to formally respond to the filing once it becomes public, and further details about the specific allegations underlying Kohberger's claim of inadequate counsel are likely to emerge as the petition proceeds through the court system in the coming weeks.

PENNSYLVANIA (WFMZ-TV) - Monroe County native Bryan Kohberger is attempting to undo his conviction in the murders of four University of Idaho students.
Kohberger has filed a petition challenging his conviction, claiming he is innocent and was misled into confessing to the killings of four students at the University of Idaho, according to the New York Times.
The criminology student was convicted last year for murdering four University of Idaho students in their home. He is currently serving four life sentences.
The New York Times says Kohberger, a Monroe County native, is now seeking to abandon his guilty plea and obtain a trial, stating he was misled into confessing to the high-profile killings.
In an interview, Kohberger told The Times he has challenged the conviction, citing concerns about how the plea deal came together.
“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” Kohberger said in a statement provided to The Times on Sunday night.
The Times says he reiterated in a phone call from prison that he had an “absolute claim of innocence.”
This interview was the first public comment Kohberger has made since the conviction, as he had not granted an interview before speaking with The Times, says the publication.
Kohberger declined to discuss any evidence or other specific details related to his innocence claim, as well as what specific concerns he had about the plea process, says The Times.
"A judge, in my opinion, is going to deny this and he's not going to get anywhere quickly," Attorney John Waldron said.
Criminal Defense Attorney John Waldron says post-conviction wins are rare.
"Admitted in writing, like I said, he admitted it orally. The judge asked him more than once, did you do this? Yes. Did you commit these crimes? Yes. So, he doesn't have a leg to stand on," Waldron said.
Kohberger made the petition from his Idaho cell, as he continues to represent himself. According to the publication, records show the filing reached the court on Monday morning. Kohberger, who had court-appointed representation throughout the case, says he has prepared the documentation to challenge the case on his own, says The Times. He will seek to have a lawyer appointed to help him going forward.
"He's sitting there doing nothing every day and he rereads his transcripts and does nothing other than to think, well, maybe they should have done this or maybe I could do this," Waldron said.
Waldron says challenging his plea creates legal risks. By claiming his original defense counsel was ineffective, Kohberger forfeits attorney-client privilege if a judge grants him a hearing.
"So, they'll take the stand, say what they did, and if they choose to, they can say what he said to them about what happened," Waldron said.
For the victim's families, the appeal reopens deep wounds. In a statement Monday, Kaylee Goncalves' family called Kohberger a 'mosquito you just can't seem to swat'.
The statement went on:
“He [Kohberger] did this after deciding not to leave his fate and the facts of the case up to a jury to decide his guilt. He never cried wolf or claimed he was uninformed, pressured, or that there were issues with the discovery that he and his counsel had for 2 years that he thought should have been challenged. He admitted to guilt and asked whether he actually was guilty he said ‘yes’.
Regardless of how this turns out, our family is 100% ready. An actual trial this time? Let's go! We are confident he will get the death penalty that he escaped by pleading guilty the first time around.”
"The families and the grief and frustration and heartbreak they've gone through, and they thought there was closure, and there should be closure," said Waldron.
Waldron warns if Kohberger succeeds in getting a trial; prosecutors also start from scratch.
"Let's say a judge took it to a hearing and says, you want a trial, Mr. Kohberger, we'll give you a trial," Waldron explained. "And then the death penalty is back on the table."
But Kohberger has his ultimate goal in sight saying justice was not served and the public demands the truth.
Kohberger was charged after his DNA was found on a knife sheath that had been left next to two of the victims. Amazon records showed he had purchased a Ka-Bar knife and sheath months prior, says The Times.
Additionally, the publication shared that the man drove a white Elantra, which is the type of car that investigators determined had been on surveillance video circling the crime scene and then speeding away from it.
Kohberger’s phone showed he was out on the night of the crime, with his phone turned off at the time of the murders.
The New York Times says Kohberger declined to discuss the evidence against him during the interview.
“The intention is for all of those questions to be investigated and answered appropriately in a trial setting,” said Kohberger.
Idaho Attorney General Raul Labrador said in a statement:
“My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana, and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news.
My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out.”

Bryan Kohberger is trying to reopen the case he ended with four guilty pleas.
On Monday, the man serving four consecutive life terms for the murders of four University of Idaho students opened a new post-conviction proceeding in Ada County and asked to withdraw his plea, setting up an effort to obtain a new trial.
The filing arrives one year after Kohberger stood before a judge and admitted killing Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin in their Moscow home.
Nothing has been reversed. His convictions and sentences remain in force, and the claims in his new affidavit are allegations that have not been tested or accepted by a court.
BREAKING: Bryan Kohberger is seeking to withdraw his guilty plea over the 2022 murders of four University of Idaho students and is asking for a new trial.
He claims his plea was based on false promises, misinformation, and ineffective legal counsel, while maintaining his… pic.twitter.com/UEK6BNFQFd
— Fox News (@FoxNews) July 27, 2026
A prison phone call with The New York Times put Kohberger’s reversal in his own voice. He maintained his innocence and portrayed the plea as the product of false promises, misinformation and ineffective legal counsel.
Kohberger declined to explain why he admitted the murders in court and would not discuss the evidence he now says supports his position. That leaves his newly filed paperwork, rather than his public statement, as the first place to examine his specific accusations.
He filed the case without an attorney under Ada County case number CV01-26-15094 and also requested appointed counsel. The public case entry identifies the matter as a Post Conviction Act proceeding and lists it as active and pending.
In a sworn affidavit, Kohberger alleges his defense team pressured him with warnings about death row and did not tell him about discovery he describes as unknown hair recovered from Ethan Chapin’s hands. No judge has ruled that evidence was withheld, exculpatory or mishandled.
Here is Bryan Kohberger's motion for Petition for Post-Conviction Relief (CV01-26-15094).
On Monday, per the New York Times, Kohberger moved to withdraw his guilty plea related to the brutal November, 2022, slaying of four University of Idaho college students named Ethan Chapin,… https://t.co/D9TMz1J1Vb pic.twitter.com/wKsRcckyBJ
— Grant Smith Ellis (@GrantSmithEllis) July 27, 2026
The written agreement filed by the Idaho District Court on July 2, 2025, preserves a starkly different record. Kohberger agreed to plead guilty to burglary and four counts of first-degree murder under terms that removed the possibility of a death sentence.
The deal called for a fixed 10-year sentence on the burglary count and four fixed life sentences on the murder counts, all running consecutively. Kohberger later received those sentences and has no possibility of parole.
Paragraph five says Kohberger acknowledged that he was not being coerced, understood the consequences and was satisfied with his legal representation. It also says he had reviewed possible defenses with counsel and voluntarily waived those defenses and related constitutional claims.
Paragraph six says he knowingly, voluntarily and intelligently waived his rights to appeal every issue in the case. The final page bears Kohberger’s signature beside those of his attorney and the prosecutors, leaving the court to decide whether his new allegations can overcome the statements he signed.
ABC News confirmed that the petition was filed Monday in Ada County, where Kohberger entered his plea and received his sentence last year. The filing begins a new challenge to the convictions; it does not itself erase them or schedule another trial.
Kohberger pleaded guilty on July 2, 2025, avoiding a capital trial that had been set to begin weeks later. Judge Steven Hippler sentenced him on July 23 to four consecutive life terms for the murders and a separate fixed term for burglary.
The new proceeding puts his claims of coercion and ineffective counsel before the same Idaho court system whose record shows him repeatedly accepting the deal. Any relief would require a court order after the legal claims and underlying evidence are examined.
As of Monday afternoon, the public material showed no order allowing Kohberger to withdraw his plea and no new trial date. The case remains a conviction under challenge, not a conviction undone.
Goncalves family statement reacting to Bryan Kohberger wanting to abandon his guilty plea. pic.twitter.com/dC6FkSsbGb
— Brian Entin (@BrianEntin) July 27, 2026
Kaylee Goncalves’s family answered the news by pointing back to the plea hearing. Kohberger had four lawyers beside him, they said, never claimed he was uninformed or pressured, and answered “Yes” when the judge asked whether he was actually guilty.
The family believes Kohberger received exactly what he requested: a deal that spared his life. They described the new challenge as another attempt to roll the dice after accepting that bargain.
Their statement also asked that far more energy be directed toward honoring the four young people whose lives were taken. The legal spotlight has returned to Kohberger, but the human center of this case has never changed.
Madison and Kaylee were 21. Xana and Ethan were 20.
Kohberger can press every claim the law permits, and the court can test those claims against the evidence and the record he signed. His new filing does not alter the four names that brought this case into the world or the families forced to endure another chapter of it.

Man convicted in Idaho college killings seeks to take back guilty plea
The criminology student convicted last year of murdering four University of Idaho students in their home is seeking to abandon his guilty plea and obtain a trial, claiming he is innocent and was misled into confessing to the high-profile killings.
In an interview with The New York Times, Bryan Kohberger, who is serving four life sentences, said he had filed a petition challenging his conviction, citing concerns about how the plea deal came together.
“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” Kohberger said in a statement provided to the Times on Sunday night. He reiterated in a phone call from prison in Idaho that he had an “absolute claim of innocence.”
Kohberger had not granted an interview or made public comments before speaking with the Times. He declined to discuss any evidence or other specific details related to his innocence claim, as well as what specific concerns he had about the plea process.
It is rare for defendants to win post-conviction challenges, which often revolve around claims of newly discovered evidence or an ineffective assistance of counsel.
Steve Goncalves, the father of one of the victims, declined to comment this morning, saying he wanted to discuss the issue with his family. The Latah County Prosecutor’s Office did not immediately return a call seeking comment.

In November 2022, the four murders in Moscow, Idaho, a college town that had not seen a homicide in seven years, captivated the country for weeks as investigators struggled to identify a suspect. Kohberger’s arrest brought relief to the community but also stoked further mystery and speculation, as investigators never identified a motive or any previous relationship with the victims.
In court, law enforcement officials outlined the evidence against Kohberger. His DNA was found on a Ka-Bar knife sheath that had been left next to two of the victims. Amazon records showed he had purchased a Ka-Bar knife and sheath months prior. He drove a white Elantra, the type of car that investigators determined had been on surveillance video circling the crime scene and then speeding away from it. Kohberger’s phone showed he was out that night, with his phone turned off at the time of the murders.
Kohberger declined to discuss the evidence against him in his call with the Times. He said, “The intention is for all of those questions to be investigated and answered appropriately in a trial setting.”
Kohberger, who had court-appointed representation throughout the case, ending with his guilty plea, said he prepared the documentation to challenge the case on his own. He will seek to have a lawyer appointed to help him going forward. Records show the filing reached the court this morning.
After he was arrested in December 2022, Kohberger’s initial lawyer said his client was eager to be exonerated. Court-appointed lawyers spent more than two years challenging the evidence collected against Kohberger, only for a surprise plea deal to come together a few weeks before a trial was to begin.
Kohberger accepted responsibility for the murders at a July 2025 hearing. He was not required to offer a motive for the killings — and never has. The lack of a detailed confession outraged some of the victims’ family members and even President Donald Trump, who had called on the judge to demand an explanation from Kohberger.
In court, the judge asked Kohberger, “Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?”
“Yes,” Kohberger responded. He later sat in silence at a sentencing hearing at which family members of the victims expressed their grief and anger.
In the early morning hours of Nov. 13, 2022, after a typical Saturday night out, the four victims were stabbed to death in an off-campus home. The bodies of Madison Mogen, 21, and Kaylee Goncalves, 21, were found together in a bed on the home’s third floor. The bodies of Xana Kernodle, 20, and her boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, 20, were found in a bedroom on the second floor.
Two surviving roommates were in a bedroom on the home’s first floor. One of them reported seeing a shadowy figure in the middle of the night and hearing a commotion. But the roommates did not seek help until later in the morning, saying they had not realized what had transpired.
One of the experts who worked on Kohberger’s defense team has taken particular issue with the plea arrangement and the evidence. Brent Turvey, a forensic scientist who analyzed the crime scene for the defense, argued that the crime was committed by multiple perpetrators, criticized how investigators documented evidence and questioned why more testing was not done of a hair found with one of the victims.
The lawyers who served as Kohberger’s defense team have rebuked Turvey, telling The Idaho Statesman that he “is now speaking about topics that are still confidential, many of which are outside of his areas of expertise.” The lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday. Turvey’s concerns were included in a book about the case, “Broken Plea.”
Kohberger alluded to those issues in his statement, saying that “unanswered questions seem to multiply with each piece of discovery unsealed.” He said he was not concerned that, if offered a new trial, he could face the death penalty.
“Why am I breaking my silence?” Kohberger said Sunday in the interview from the Idaho Maximum Security Institution, just south of Boise. “A lot went wrong in those plea discussions. I really do want that to be heard.”
Kohberger grew up in Pennsylvania and moved to Pullman, Washington, in 2022 to pursue a doctorate in the criminal justice and criminology program at Washington State University, just across the state border from the University of Idaho. He had long been interested in serial killers and the minds of criminals.
Kohberger had signed a plea agreement agreeing that he “knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently waives all rights to appeal any and all issues in this case.” Still, defendants can make other claims about the legal process through post-conviction relief.

A petition filed in Ada County Court on Monday confirmed Kohberger's effort to withdraw his guilty plea and expanded on his reasoning. Kohberger argued that he was convinced by his counsel that actual guilt wasn't relevant to his plea and that his guilty plea was necessary to avoid the death penalty. He also argued that his attorneys ignored exculpatory evidence.
Kohberger pleaded guilty to the killings in July of 2025, more than two years after the killings. His guilty plea and the terms of his agreement with prosecutors were considered in a public hearing by Ada County Judge Steven Hippler. Hippler signed off on the agreement after Kohberger confirmed that he was guilty of the crime and that he was properly represented.
Those statements by Kohberger after his attorneys reached the agreement with prosecutors pose an obstacle for his new efforts to retract his plea, but a reversal is possible if he can prove he was improperly represented or present new evidence.
In his petition asking to take back his guilty plea, Kohberger cited "clumps of unknown hair found in Ethan Chapin's hand" as exculpatory evidence brought up in the plea discussions that he wasn't told about.
Additionally, he claimed that his attorneys convinced him that "actual guilt was not an important factor in considering plea acceptance."
He also wrote that he was lied to about the conditions of living on death row.
Attorney Kevin Curtis said that the burden of proof Kohberger would have to meet should the judge choose to get more information would be incredibly high.
"So for the defendant now to come back and say, 'Hey, listen, there were promises made. There's duress or was ineffective assistance of counsel. Counsel lied to me. They told me that I didn't have to be guilty to plead guilty and say I was guilty.' He's got almost an insurmountable burden to be able to withdraw this plea," Curtis said.
From his reading of the filing, Curtis doesn't believe the evidence will meet the burden.
"I don't think what he raises in the petition, as for the clump of hair, rises anywhere near the level of exculpatory evidence that one would expect, could merit a reversal or withdrawal," Curtis said.
According to Curtis, the judge has several options now that the petition for conviction relief has been filed.

"Or you can say we're going to go to a next step, which doesn't mean he's granting the petition and allowing the withdrawal of plea, but he thinks there might be at least enough substance to explore the allegations further through hearings or through further documents to make a final determination."
The judge has 30 days to make the decision.
If he does choose to request more information, the state would also be able to question Kohberger's attorneys, as attorney-client privilege would be gone, Curtis explained.
A reversal of his guilty plea wouldn't guarantee him a better outcome. At the time when his plea agreement was announced, members of at least one of the families of the victims were outraged that the Latah County Prosecutor's Office accepted the deal that took the death penalty off the table.

sources.text:
In a dramatic shift from his formal admission of guilt, Bryan Kohberger has publicly declared his intention to retract his guilty plea in the 2022 slayings of four University of Idaho students.
In a statement released on July 26, Kohberger asserted his "actual innocence," alleging that his guilty plea was hinged on false promises and blatant disinformation. Claiming that justice was not served and describing the prosecution's case as a "myopic narrative work of fiction," Kohberger stated he welcomes a full trial and is even prepared to face the death penalty once again.
The sudden declaration comes roughly a year after Kohberger agreed to four consecutive life sentences without parole to avoid capital punishment. However, translating a post-sentencing statement into an actual vacated conviction presents an extraordinarily steep legal hurdle under Idaho law.
Newsweek has reached out to Kohbeger's attorney and Moscow Police Department Chief Anthony Dahlinger for comment. Latah County Prosecutor’s Office said it could not comment on pending litigation.
Kristi Goncalves, 48, the mother of victim Kaylee, told Newsweek in an exclusive interview that she believed Kohberger was playing "games."
“America has seen our family go through pain for many, many years now," she told Newsweek. "It wasn’t the news we wanted to wake up to today. It's just games, it's just judicial games. We don't think there's any merit to it at all."
Idaho Attorney General, Raúl R. Labrador, said in a statement Monday that his office was ready to do "whatever is necessary" to ensure justice was carried out.
"My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana, and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news," he said in a statement on X. "My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out."
What the Law Says
The legal mechanisms governing guilty pleas in Idaho depend heavily on timing.
Under Idaho Rule of Criminal Procedure 33(c), requests made prior to sentencing are evaluated under a relatively lenient standard that allows withdrawal for any fair and just reason. Once a judge has formally imposed a sentence, however, the standard shifts dramatically. Post-sentencing withdrawals are permitted only to correct a manifest injustice. Because Kohberger has already been sentenced, his legal team must convince the court that leaving his original conviction intact would result in a clear, fundamental miscarriage of justice.
Proving a manifest injustice requires meeting a high evidentiary bar. Courts typically consider a plea vulnerable only if the defendant can show that it was entered involuntarily, that defense counsel provided constitutionally ineffective assistance, or that prosecutorial misconduct prejudiced the outcome. While Kohberger's public statement claims he was misled by false promises and disinformation, he previously affirmed under oath during his change-of-plea hearing before Judge Steven Hippler that he understood the agreement, was acting voluntarily, and was entering the plea because he was in fact guilty. Overcoming those sworn statements in open court will require substantial, concrete evidence rather than broad assertions.
Complicating matters further is the legal framework surrounding post-conviction appeals.
As part of his original plea agreement, Kohberger formally waived his right to a direct appeal. While such waivers do not entirely bar post-conviction petitions based on severe constitutional violations or newly discovered evidence, courts view post-sentence retractions with profound skepticism. Unless his defense team can present tangible proof of coercion, fraud, or egregious errors that directly corrupted the plea process, legal observers emphasize that courts rarely overturn a settled guilty plea at this stage.
The Idaho Post-Conviction Procedure Act Explained
In Idaho, once a criminal defendant has been sentenced and exhausted or waived their direct appeal rights, the primary legal avenue to challenge a conviction is through the Uniform Post-Conviction Procedure Act (Idaho Code § 19-4901 et seq.). Unlike a direct appeal—which only reviews the existing record for legal errors made by the judge—a post-conviction petition initiates a separate, civil proceeding. This framework allows a defendant to introduce new evidence or raise constitutional claims that were not fully developed on the record during the original plea or trial proceedings.
Because a post-conviction petition is legally classified as a civil action, the burden of proof rests entirely on the petitioner to establish their claims by a preponderance of the evidence. Common grounds for relief under the Act include substantial constitutional violations, such as ineffective assistance of counsel, coerced guilty pleas, or prosecutorial misconduct, as well as newly discovered evidence that could not have been uncovered before sentencing through due diligence. However, Idaho courts enforce a strict one-year statute of limitations from the final judgment, and judges evaluate these post-conviction claims with deep skepticism when a defendant attempts to overturn a plea they previously affirmed under oath.
Kohberger's Statement in Full
In a statement, provided to the New York Times via his family, Kohberger wrote:
"Over year later it is self evident that in State v Kohberger, justice was not served; unanswered questions seem to multiply with each piece of discovery unsealed and the public demands the truth.
Unfortunately the truth shall never be derived from the State's myopic narrative work of fiction which has yet to evolve since the PCA was released nearly years ago and its faulty premises were never challenged at trial.
Circumnavigated by broken plea the trial never provided the public the clarity conducive to closure and justice shall remain abjectly miscarried unless that plea is withdrawn hereby declare my intention to enter not guilty plea and welcome the State the opportunity to prove their case at trial as well as to again file for the death penalty. My actual innocence is my truth and the plea hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation MUST be withdrawn.
Thank you for all who believe in my innocence and continue to critically analyze the case send my love to my family who have never wavered in their belief in who am their belief in my innocence."
When Was Bryan Kohberger Sentenced?
Kohberger was formally sentenced on July 23, 2025, in the Ada County Courthouse in Boise, Idaho. Three weeks prior, on July 2, 2025, Kohberger entered a surprise guilty plea to four counts of first-degree murder and one count of felony burglary as part of a negotiated agreement to avoid the death penalty.
Hippler sentenced Kohberger to four consecutive fixed life terms in prison without the possibility of parole, alongside an additional 10-year sentence for the burglary charge. During the emotional, daylong hearing, family members of the victims delivered impact statements confronting Kohberger directly, while Kohberger declined to address the court before his sentence was imposed.
What We Know About Bryan Kohberger's Family
Kohberger grew up in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, raised by his parents, Michael and Maryann Kohberger, alongside two older sisters, Amanda and Melissa. Prior to his arrest, his family lived in Albrightsville, Pennsylvania, where his father worked in maintenance and his mother worked as a educational paraprofessional. Both of his sisters pursued careers in behavioral health and psychology.
Throughout the legal proceedings, Kohberger's family has maintained a quiet presence, releasing an initial statement in early 2023 expressing empathy for the victims' families while supporting Bryan through the judicial process. Kohberger's family attended several court hearings in Idaho following his extradition, and his latest statement explicitly thanked them for their continued, unwavering belief in his innocence.
Who Were the Victims of the Idaho Murders?
The four victims were University of Idaho students who were brutally stabbed to death in their off-campus rental home on King Road in Moscow, Idaho, on November 13, 2022.
- Kaylee Goncalves, 21: A senior general studies major from Rathdrum, Idaho, preparing to graduate early with plans to move to Austin, Texas, for an IT career.

- Xana Kernodle, 20: A junior marketing major from Post Falls, Idaho, remembered for her energetic personality and active role in her sorority, Pi Beta Phi.
- Ethan Chapin, 20: A freshman sports management major from Conway, Washington, and member of the Sigma Chi fraternity, who was staying at the house as Kernodle’s boyfriend.

Bryan Kohberger trying to challenge conviction in University of Idaho murders: Court documents
(BOISE, Idaho) -- Bryan Kohberger, who pleaded guilty last year to the University of Idaho murders, is trying to challenge his conviction, according to new court documents.
Kohberger filed a petition on Monday for post-conviction relief with the Ada County District Court. He is currently representing himself, according to the docket.
The family of victim Kaylee Goncalves said in a statement Monday that Kohberger admitted his guilt in his plea and "chose not to leave his fate -- or the facts of the case -- to a jury."
"We would have preferred a death-penalty trial; we believe fully in the evidence," the family said. "Instead, [Kohberger] received exactly what he asked for: a deal that spared his life. Know this -- he hates that life. He wants another chance to roll the dice."
If Kohberger is granted a hearing, the family said that day in court will offer him a "welcome break from solitary confinement: a ride, perhaps different food, photos taken, and the spotlight once again fixed on him and his supposed 'innocence.'"
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said in a statement Monday, "My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana, and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today's deeply painful news. My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out."
Kohberger was arrested for the stabbing deaths of four University of Idaho students -- roommates Kaylee Goncalves, Madison Mogen and Xana Kernodle, and Kernodle's boyfriend, Ethan Chapin -- at the girls' off-campus house in 2022.
DNA from a knife sheath left at the crime scene was found to be a "statistical match" to Kohberger, authorities said. Kohberger's phone was also near the victims' house at least 12 times before the murders, court documents said, with all of those times, except for one, late at night or early in the morning.
In July 2025, weeks before his trial was set to start, Kohberger pleaded guilty to all counts. As part of the plea deal, the death penalty was taken off the table.
Kohberger was given four consecutive life sentences for four first-degree murder counts as well as 10 years for the burglary count. Kohberger -- a criminology student at Washington State University at the time of the murders -- didn't address the court at sentencing.
Authorities said last year that the motive remained unknown and they didn't know which victim was the specific target.
